title: That by which one knows
theme: That by which one knows form, taste, smell, sounds, touches and the pleasures of union — by this alone one knows; what is left here? This is that.

sandhi.rule: Final m → anusvāra before a consonant, P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).
Final n before c becomes ṃś (anusvāra and ś), P. 8.3.7 (नश्छव्यप्रशान्).
Final t becomes d before a voiced sound, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते).

morphology.note: A derivative of mithuna ‘pair’: what belongs to union. The masculine plural agrees in form with śabdān and sparśān; the commentators gloss it as the pleasures that arise from union.
Present passive of śiṣ ‘leave’ with pari: ‘is left over, remains’.
With vai tat, the refrain that closes this verse and the following ones: ‘this, truly, is that’ — this self is what was asked about.

translation.literal: ‘That by which [one knows] form, taste, smell, sounds and touches and the [pleasures] of union — by this alone one knows. What is left over here? This, truly, is that.’
translation.readable: ‘It is by this that one knows colour and taste and smell, sounds and touch and the joys of love. What is there that it does not know? This is what you asked about.’

anvaya: येन [आत्मना] रूपम् रसम् गन्धम् शब्दान् स्पर्शान् मैथुनान् च [लोकः विजानाति], एतेन एव विजानाति । अत्र किम् परिशिष्यते ? एतत् वै तत् ॥
syntax: A relative clause (yena …) whose verb is supplied from the main clause, picked up by etenaiva vijānāti; then a rhetorical question (kim atra pariśiṣyate) and the refrain etad vai tat, a nominal sentence.

ambiguities.topic: What does ‘what is left here?’ ask?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: nothing is left that this self does not know, so it is all-knowing, «स आत्मा सर्वज्ञः». Raṅgarāmānuja: what is there that it does not illumine, «किं तत् अप्रकाश्यम् ? इति भावः».

Śaṅkara: what Naciketas asked about, which even the gods doubted, «यन्नचिकेतसा पृष्टं देवादिभिरपि विचिकित्सितं», the highest place of Viṣṇu. Raṅgarāmānuja: the highest place named earlier as the goal, «पूर्वं प्राप्यतया निर्दिष्टं तत्परमं पदं».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Two half-lines of 16 syllables (four pādas of eight), followed by the refrain etad vai tat, four syllables, which also closes 2.1.5–2.1.8.

beginner: This verse asks a quiet question. Think of everything you know through the senses: colours, tastes, smells, sounds, the feel of things, the pleasures of love. Each is known by something — not by the eye or the tongue on its own, but by the awareness that uses them. That awareness is what the verse points to. Śaṅkara gives an argument: if the body, which is itself made of colours, textures and the rest, could know them, then a stone or a flower should be able to know its own colour too, and it cannot. So the knower must be something other than what it knows. Then the verse asks: what is left that this does not know? Nothing. And it ends with a refrain that will return several times: this, truly, is that — the very thing Naciketas asked about.
analogy: A lamp that shows every object in a room; one does not need another lamp to see the lamp.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That by which one knows every object of the senses — this alone is the knower; nothing is left that it does not know. This is that.

commentary.q: Why the body is not the knower
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara grants that people think ‘I, the body, know’, and answers: if what is itself form and the rest could know form, then outer things should know one another and themselves, «तर्हि बाह्या अपि रूपादयोऽन्योन्यं स्वं स्वं रूपं च विजानीयुः»; they do not, so it is the self, other than the body, that knows. Nothing is left unknown to it, so it is all-knowing, «स आत्मा सर्वज्ञः».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the senses act by its favour
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The senses that show form and the rest begin their work only as favoured by it, «रूपादिप्रकाशकानाम् इन्द्रियाणां तदनुगृहीतानामेव कार्यारम्भकत्वात् इति भावः»; he cites a line of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka in support (‘the light of lights’). ‘This is that’: this self taught in the verse is the highest place named before, «एतन्मन्त्रप्रतिपाद्यात्मस्वरूपमेव इत्यर्थः».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: etad vai tat is printed as a short line of its own. It closes this verse and the five that follow, and ties each description back to the question Naciketas asked.

advaita.text: The knower is the self whose nature is consciousness, other than the body, «देहादिव्यतिरिक्तेनैव विज्ञानस्वभावेनात्मना»; ‘this is that’: this self is the highest place of Viṣṇu that Naciketas asked about.

visistadvaita.text: The senses work only as favoured by the self (with the Supreme as the light of lights); ‘this is that’ identifies the self taught here with the goal named before, «पूर्वं प्राप्यतया निर्दिष्टं तत्परमं पदं».

schools.disagreement: Both read ‘that’ as the goal Naciketas asked about; for Śaṅkara the knower of all objects is itself that goal, while Raṅgarāmānuja grounds the senses’ work in a light beyond them. In our source Madhva’s bhāṣya has no comment on this verse (see flags).

parallels.note: ‘The light of lights’: Raṅgarāmānuja cites the line here (his reference reads 6.4.16) to show that the senses illumine only by that light.

contemporary.text: Everything we experience comes with someone experiencing it, and that one is the easiest thing to overlook. The verse simply asks us to notice it. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: Name five things you are aware of right now. What is aware of all five?
reflect.deeper: Why does Śaṅkara think that what is known cannot itself be the knower?
reflect.practice: While eating something, notice the taste, and then notice the noticing.

flags.note: GRETIL keys स्पर्शींश्, a witness error for sparśān (corrections.json).
madhva.json files under 2.1.2–2.1.3 a comment beginning with the words of 2.2.6 (इदं गुह्यं ब्रह्म प्रवक्ष्यामि); it is not quoted as a gloss on this verse.
